title: Why Arjuna can't sit out
hookLine: three roads open at once, and the first one starts with Arjuna asking why he can't just walk away
carry: karma yoga: not whether you act, but how
tomorrow: bhakti: the butter thief and the rope that was always too short

lines: A DAY ON EACH, IN TURNS.
cards: A man on a battlefield wants to stop acting. Arjuna has just heard Krishna praise wisdom and calm, so he asks the obvious question: if understanding is higher than action, why are you pushing me into this terrible work?
That's where the first road starts. Hindus often speak of three great roads. Karma: action.
Bhakti: devotion. Jnana: knowledge. Teachers often say a person leans toward one.
For the next three weeks, this path takes them in turns, a day on each, around and around, so whichever road is yours, you'll walk it, and you'll meet the other two as neighbors.

teach.b: That's how the Gita's third chapter opens. You read it once, back in the Gita camp; now, slower. And it's a fair confusion.
In chapter two Krishna described the wise person as steady and unshaken. Arjuna hears that and thinks: great, then let me sit down, be wise, and skip the fighting. Krishna's answer is practical.

teach.h: NO ONE IS ACTIONLESS, EVEN FOR A MOMENT.
teach.b: No one, he says, can remain even for a moment without acting. Breathing is action. Thinking is action.
Sitting still with your arms folded is a decision, and decisions are action. Not starting something doesn't make you free of action.
And if you sit with your hands still while your mind races after what you've given up, Krishna calls that pretending. So, he says, do the work that's yours.
Action is better than inaction. Even keeping your body alive would be impossible without it. This is the ground of karma yoga, and it takes the pressure off in a strange way.

teach.h: NOT WHETHER YOU'LL ACT, BUT HOW.
teach.b: The question is never whether you'll act.

teach.h: NA HI KAŚCIT KṢAṆAM API JĀTU TIṢṬHATY AKARMA-KṚT.
teach.b: You're acting right now, by listening. The only question is how: with grasping, or as an offering; with your whole self, or with half your mind somewhere else.
Staying silent in an argument, skipping a prayer so you can't do it wrong: those are actions too. Karma, the word, just means action, from a root meaning to do.

how: Many Hindus describe three great paths, karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge), and lean toward one; the Gita's third chapter is the classic teaching on karma yoga, often studied chapter by chapter in homes and study circles.

action, anything you do, even thinking
a duty handed to you at birth

games.q: the three roads, and chapter three — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna tells Arjuna the wise stop acting
he says no one can remain even for a moment without acting.
in chapter three, Krishna says action is better than inaction
and even keeping the body alive would be impossible without it.
it means action, from the root kri, to do.

games.q: you're Arjuna. Krishna has praised calm wisdom. you'd rather sit down than fight. what does Krishna say?
o: yes, sit down: wisdom means doing nothing.
no one can be without action, even for a moment. do your work.
go home and think about it.
games.why: no one is ever actionless. the question isn't whether you'll act, but how: that's the beginning of karma yoga.

practice: Notice how much is being done right now without your deciding: the heart beating, the lungs filling, the eyes adjusting to the light, so that even stillness is full of action.
Breathe in and feel the body working for you; breathe out a small thank you, then bring to mind one piece of work waiting for you and picture yourself doing it with your whole attention.
If you pray, you can offer that work before you begin it.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first road of the three, and the Gita's third chapter says no one ever stops walking it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: action, deed, work; from the root kri, to do.

carryVoice: Carry this: karma yoga, not whether you act, but how. Even avoiding something is an action. See you on the bhakti road tomorrow.
